# Part 1 · Setup and Data

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and Data ───────────────────────────────────────────
library(janitor)
library(tidyverse)

g_df <- read_csv("data/gray_I3_I8.csv")

i3_df <- g_df %>% filter(lake == "I3")

head(g_df)
```

**▶ Run this** — the three numbers everything today depends on:

``` r
# ── Part 1.2 · Setup and Data ───────────────────────────────────────────
stats_df <- g_df %>%
  group_by(lake) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_length = mean(length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_length   = sd(length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    n           = sum(!is.na(length_mm)),
    se_length   = sd_length / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
stats_df
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which lake has more fish measured? Which has the larger mean length? Which has the larger SD? `________________________`

## A tool you will reuse all semester

You just typed out `mean`, `sd`, `n` and `se` by hand. You will want those same four numbers in *every* analysis from here on — so let's package them into a **function** and never type that block again.

::: callout-note
**This one is a tool, not a lesson — it is already filled in for you in the script skeleton.** You do not have to type it. Read it, run it, and then use it.

`{{ variable }}` (the "curly-curly" braces) is what lets you hand the function a *bare column name* like `length_mm` instead of a quoted string. It is the one piece of syntax here worth remembering.
:::

**▶ Run this** — define it once:

``` r
# ── Part 1.3 · A reusable summary function ──────────────────────────────
summary_stats <- function(data, variable) {
  data %>%
    summarize(
      n        = sum(!is.na({{ variable }})),
      mean     = mean({{ variable }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd       = sd({{ variable }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      se       = sd / sqrt(n),
      ci_lower = mean - qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
      ci_upper = mean + qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(across(c(mean, sd, se, ci_lower, ci_upper),
                  ~ round_half_up(.x, 2)))
}
```

**▶ Run this** — now use it. Three ways, no retyping:

``` r
# ── Part 1.4 · A reusable summary function ──────────────────────────────
g_df %>% group_by(lake) %>% summary_stats(length_mm)   # per lake

g_df %>% summary_stats(length_mm)                      # both lakes pooled

g_df %>% group_by(lake) %>% summary_stats(mass_g)      # a different column
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Compare the first result to `stats_df` from Part 1.2. Do the `mean`, `sd` and `se` columns match? `________________________`

✏️ **Your turn:** The function also returns `ci_lower` and `ci_upper` — a 95% confidence interval. We have not explained those yet. **That is Part 6.** For now, just notice they are there.

# Part 2 · The Normal Distribution

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 10 (The Normal Distribution); Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 2.

A normal distribution is fully described by just two numbers: its mean (μ) and its standard deviation (σ). Let's draw the normal curve that matches our fish and see how well it fits.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 2.1 · The Normal Distribution ──────────────────────────────────
i3_mean <- mean(i3_df$length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
i3_sd   <- sd(i3_df$length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)

i3_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 10,
                 fill = "lightblue", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = i3_mean, sd = i3_sd),
                colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Length (mm)", y = "Density")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Where does the red curve sit **above** the blue bars, and where does it sit **below** them? Look especially at the right-hand side. `________________________`

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 3 · Z-Scores — Putting Everything on One Ruler

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 10 — standardizing a value.

There is a different normal curve for every μ and σ. Standardizing rescales any of them into the *same* units: standard deviations from the mean.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 3.1 · Z-Scores ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
i3_df <- i3_df %>%
  mutate(z_score = (length_mm - i3_mean) / i3_sd)

i3_df %>%
  select(lake, length_mm, z_score) %>%
  head()

i3_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = z_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "blue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "z (SDs from the mean)", y = "Count")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Compare this histogram to the one in Part 2. What changed — the **shape**, or just the **axis numbers**? `________________________`

**▶ Run this** — what fraction of our fish really are within 1 SD?

``` r
# ── Part 3.2 · Z-Scores ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
within_1sd <- mean(abs(i3_df$z_score) <= 1, na.rm = TRUE)
round_half_up(100 * within_1sd, 1)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** A perfect normal distribution gives 68%. What did you get, and is the gap big or small? `________________________`

# Part 4 · Area Under the Curve = Probability

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 5 (Probability) and Ch. 10.

The whole point of a density curve is that **area under it is probability**. `pnorm()` gives us that area without any integration.

| Function | You give it | You get back |
|----|----|----|
| `pnorm(z)` | a **z** | the **area to the left** |
| `qnorm(p)` | an **area** | the **z** that cuts it off |
| `dnorm(z)` | a **z** | the **height** of the curve |

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · Area Under the Curve ─────────────────────────────────────
pnorm(1.96)          # area to the LEFT of 1.96
1 - pnorm(1.96)      # area to the RIGHT
qnorm(0.975)         # the z with 97.5% to its left - the inverse of pnorm
```

**▶ Run this** — the worked example from lecture: how rare is a 300 mm grayling?

``` r
# ── Part 4.2 · Area Under the Curve ─────────────────────────────────────
z_300 <- (300 - i3_mean) / i3_sd
round_half_up(z_300, 2)                          # should be about 1.22

round_half_up(100 * (1 - pnorm(z_300)), 1)       # % of fish LONGER than 300 mm
```

**▶ Run this** — and now run it backwards, from a probability to a length:

``` r
# ── Part 4.3 · Area Under the Curve ─────────────────────────────────────
z_top5 <- qnorm(0.95)
length_top5 <- i3_mean + z_top5 * i3_sd
round_half_up(length_top5, 1)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** In one sentence, what does that last number mean to someone fishing lake I3? `________________________`

✏️ **Your turn:** Use `pnorm()` to find the percentage of I3 fish shorter than **240 mm**. Convert 240 to a z-score first.


::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early:** Shade the tail you just calculated.

``` r
  geom_vline(xintercept = 300, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed")
```

# Part 5 · Checking the Assumption

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 13 (Handling Violations of Assumptions).

Every number in Part 4 assumed the fish are normally distributed. Now we test that.

**Watch the hypotheses — they run backwards from what you expect:**

- **H₀: the data ARE normal**
- **Hₐ: the data are NOT normal**
- so **p < 0.05 means NOT normal** — a small p-value here is bad news

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · Checking the Assumption ──────────────────────────────────
shapiro.test(i3_df$length_mm)

i3_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(sample = length_mm)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** What is the p-value, and what does it say about normality? On the Q-Q plot, where do the points leave the red line? `________________________`

**▶ Run this** — so how wrong was our 300 mm answer? Compare theory to the actual fish:

``` r
# ── Part 5.2 · Checking the Assumption ──────────────────────────────────
round_half_up(100 * (1 - pnorm(300, i3_mean, i3_sd)), 1)   # normal theory
round_half_up(100 * mean(i3_df$length_mm > 300, na.rm = TRUE), 1)  # actual fish
```

✏️ **Your turn:** How far apart are those two numbers? Why does it matter that the disagreement is out in the **tail** rather than in the middle? `________________________`

::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early:** Run `shapiro.test()` on lake I8 as well. Is it normal? Does the Q-Q plot agree with the p-value?

# Part 6 · SD, SE, and Confidence Intervals

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 4 (Estimating with Uncertainty) — this is the chapter that separates SD from SE.

**SD** describes how much *individual fish* vary. **SE** describes how much a *sample mean* would vary from study to study. They answer different questions and must not be swapped.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 6.1 · SD, SE, and Confidence Intervals ─────────────────────────
i3_n  <- sum(!is.na(i3_df$length_mm))
i3_se <- i3_sd / sqrt(i3_n)

tibble(
  n  = i3_n,
  SD = round_half_up(i3_sd, 1),
  SE = round_half_up(i3_se, 1)
)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** If we measured 4× as many fish, which of those two numbers would shrink, and by how much? `________________________`

**▶ Run this** — build a 95% CI by hand, the way the formula reads: $\bar{y} \pm t \cdot SE$

``` r
# ── Part 6.2 · SD, SE, and Confidence Intervals ─────────────────────────
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = i3_n - 1)   # two-tailed, 95%
t_crit

ci_lower <- i3_mean - t_crit * i3_se
ci_upper <- i3_mean + t_crit * i3_se

round_half_up(c(ci_lower, ci_upper), 1)
```

**▶ Run this** — now check yourself two ways: against R's `t.test()`, and against the function you wrote back in Part 1.3.

``` r
# ── Part 6.3 · SD, SE, and Confidence Intervals ─────────────────────────
t.test(i3_df$length_mm)$conf.int          # R's answer

i3_df %>% summary_stats(length_mm)        # your function's answer
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Do all three intervals — yours by hand, `t.test()`, and `summary_stats()` — agree? `________________________`

> 💡 **That is the payoff.** The `ci_lower` / `ci_upper` columns were in your function's output back in Part 1.4, before you knew what they meant. Now you do — and you get them on any grouped dataset for free:
>
> ``` r
> g_df %>% group_by(lake) %>% summary_stats(length_mm)
> ```
>
> One line, and every lake gets a mean, an SE, and a confidence interval.

✏️ **Your turn:** Write the I3 interval as a sentence you could put in a paper. `________________________`

**▶ Run this** — why t and not 1.96? Take a small sample and watch the multiplier change:

``` r
# ── Part 6.4 · SD, SE, and Confidence Intervals ─────────────────────────
set.seed(42)
small_sample <- i3_df %>% slice_sample(n = 10)

s_mean <- mean(small_sample$length_mm)
s_se   <- sd(small_sample$length_mm) / sqrt(10)

tibble(
  method = c("z (wrong here)", "t (correct)"),
  crit   = round_half_up(c(1.96, qt(0.975, df = 9)), 3),
  lower  = round_half_up(s_mean - crit * s_se, 1),
  upper  = round_half_up(s_mean + crit * s_se, 1),
  width  = round_half_up(upper - lower, 1)
)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which interval is wider, and why is the wider one the *honest* one? `________________________`

::: callout-note
**The interpretation to get right**

❌ "There is a 95% chance μ is in my interval."
✅ "95% of intervals built this way capture μ."

μ is a fixed number. The **interval** is what is random.
:::

# Part 7 · One-Sample t-Test

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 11 (Inference for a Normal Population) and Ch. 6 (Hypothesis Testing).

A CI asks *where is μ?* A t-test asks *is μ equal to some specific value?*

**▶ Run this** — do I3 fish differ from a historical mean of 260 mm?

``` r
# ── Part 7.1 · One-Sample t-Test ────────────────────────────────────────
t.test(i3_df$length_mm, mu = 260)
```

```
t             = __________    df = __________
p-value       = __________

```

# Part 8 · Two-Sample t-Test

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 12 (Comparing Two Means) and Ch. 6 on one- vs. two-tailed tests.

**Formulate the hypotheses first**, for the question "Are fish in Lake I8 longer than fish in Lake I3?"

```
H0 = ________________________________________________________
Ha = ________________________________________________________
```

This question has a **direction**, so it is one-tailed. R orders `lake` alphabetically and tests I3 − I8, so "I8 is longer" means that difference is **less** than zero.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 8.1 · Two-Sample t-Test ────────────────────────────────────────
t.test(length_mm ~ lake, data = g_df, alternative = "less")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** What do you conclude? Report the **difference in mm**, not just the p-value. `________________________`

✏️ **Your turn:** The output says "Welch Two Sample t-test". Look back at the SDs in Part 1.2. Why is Welch the right default here? `________________________`

# Getting unstuck

When code breaks — and it will, that is normal:

1. **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2. **Check the usual suspects:** did you run `library(tidyverse)` and `library(janitor)`? Spelling? A missing `)` or a `%>%` at the *start* of a line instead of the end?
3. `?function_name` opens the built-in help page.
4. **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class or office hours.

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §8 — Workflow: getting help](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-help.html).

> 💡 **Key idea:** Every working scientist googles error messages daily. Getting stuck is not failing — it is the job.
